decision: Booking a mock works like hailing a ride: a map of who is online, one request panel, a matching animation, then a sheet with the mentor, an ETA and progress
why: Scheduling a mock days ahead is where practice dies; the ride-hailing pattern makes 'now' the default and shows supply before you ask.
alternative: A mentor directory with calendar slots.
value: A live mock in minutes instead of days (median time to mock, target [value]).

decision: Who is online comes from each mentor's local time on the world clock (07:00–23:00), so scrubbing the clock changes the map
why: Availability follows time zones; faking a static 'online' list would hide the real constraint for someone in São Paulo.
value: The map explains why evenings are easier to match.

decision: A surge multiplier applies while US and European demand overlap, shown before you request, and credits are charged only if the mock starts
why: Demand spikes are real; showing the price up front and charging on start keeps surge from feeling like a trap.
alternative: Flat pricing with long queues at peak.
value: Peak demand spreads out, and nobody pays for a no-show.

decision: Matching is shown with expanding rings from the member and a route drawn from the matched mentor, both SVG transforms that stop under reduced motion
why: Waiting feels shorter when progress is visible; a spinner says nothing about what is happening.
value: The 2-second match reads as work being done, with no animation library.

decision: If a mentor cancels, Atlas rematches automatically with the next best mentor; if nobody is free, the member joins a waitlist with an estimated wait
why: Cancellations and empty supply are normal states of a marketplace; each gets a designed path instead of an error.
alternative: Send the member back to the start with an apology.
value: No dead ends: every request ends in a mock, a rematch or a place in line.
